title: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in annular superfluids across the UFG-BCS crossover
authors: Michał Śliwiński, Klejdja Xhani, Gabriel Wlazłowski
abstract: We investigate the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability of counter-rotating annular Fermi superfluids using time-dependent superfluid density functional theory. When the two initially separated superflows merge, a necklace of quantized vortices forms at their interface and subsequently becomes unstable. We extract mode-resolved instability growth rates and study their dependence on relative flow velocity, interaction strength, and temperature across the strongly interacting unitary regime and the weakly attractive BCS regime. In the unitary gas and moderate BCS regimes, the growth rates remain qualitatively consistent with the point-vortex model, though systematically at or above its predictions, with no significant dependence on interaction strength or temperature up to approximately $0.3 T_c$. Deeper in the BCS regime, the dynamics change qualitatively: boundary-generated antivortices proliferate faster than the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability itself, destroying the initial vortex necklace before the instability can fully develop. These results provide a microscopic benchmark for Kelvin-Helmholtz dynamics in fermionic superfluids and help constrain possible explanations of the existing experiment-theory discrepancy.
summary: The authors study the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in annular Fermi superfluids across the UFG-BCS crossover using time-dependent superfluid density functional theory. They find that while the instability growth rates match predictions in the unitary regime, the dynamics fundamentally change in the BCS regime due to competing anti-vortex proliferation. This offers crucial insights into the non-ideal, fermionic nature of superfluid dynamics.
main_problem: Investigating the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) in annular superfluids across the Unitary Fermi Gas (UFG) to Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) crossover.
main_result: The KHI growth rates are qualitatively consistent with point-vortex models in UFG/moderate BCS regimes but systematically higher. In the deep BCS regime, the dynamics change due to faster proliferation of boundary-generated antivortices, which destroys the initial vortex necklace.
method: Time-dependent superfluid density functional theory (TDSLDA) is used to simulate the real-time evolution of the superfluid system.
model_or_system: The system consists of counter-rotating annular Fermi superfluids, modeled using a time-dependent extension of the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. The analysis spans the crossover from strongly interacting UFG to weakly attractive BCS regimes.
key_observables: KHI growth rate ($\sigma$), characteristic timescale ($	au_{KHI}$), structure factor $S(m, t)$, and the density/order parameter evolution.
important_parameters: Relative flow velocity ($\Delta v$), interaction strength (parametrized by $\xi_{aF}^{-1}$), and temperature (up to $0.3 T_c$).
main_assumptions: The use of TDSLDA functional theory, which handles contact interactions via regularization; the initial state is assumed to be an idealized vortex necklace.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the stages of KHI, show the exponential growth of the structure factor $S(m, t)$ over time, and depict the qualitative change in dynamics in the deep BCS regime due to anti-vortex proliferation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework using TDSLDA, simulates the initial vortex necklace formation, analyzes the KHI growth rates across different interaction regimes (UFG $	o$ BCS), and finally details the qualitative change in dynamics observed in the deep BCS regime.
why_interesting: This work provides a microscopic, fermionic benchmark for understanding hydrodynamic instabilities in quantum superfluids, directly addressing discrepancies between theory and experiment in a highly tunable quantum system.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Sketch of distinct stages of superfluid Kelvin–Helmholtz instability in circular geometry. a) Two superfluids, separated by a barrier (dotted line), counter-rotate. b) Once the barrier is removed, a shear layer forms at the interface, giving rise to a necklace of same-sign quantized vortices (black dots). c) The vortex necklace loses its ordered structure, marking the onset of the instability.

Figure 2: Initial state representing a unitary Fermi gas (T ≈0.3 Tc) confined in a ring geometry. The Gaussian barrier separating the two superfluids has a width skF = 2.36. The imprinted current in each superfluid corresponds to a winding number w = ±6, giving a relative winding number ∆w = 12. The panels show the total density n (a), the absolute value of the order parameter |∆| (b), the external repulsive potential Vext with the current density j displayed with arrows (c), and the phase of the order parameter arg[∆] (d). VisIt software was used to generate these plots [38].

Figure 3: Formation of a vortex necklace in a unitary Fermi gas and the subsequent Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. The consecutive panels show snapshots of the system at increasing times, during and after the barrier removal, namely: a) tεF = 0, b) tεF = 56, c) tεF = 84, d) tεF = 189, e) tεF = 500, f) tεF = 1589. The color maps display the distribution of |∆(x, y)|/εF. The setup is the same as in Fig. 2. The barrier is removed in time interval ∆trεF = 60. In the pairing field profile, one can also observe a sound wave propagating towards the boundaries, visible well in panels c and d.

Figure 4: a) Temporal evolution of the structure factor for mode m=6, shown on a logarithmic scale. The shaded area indicates the time interval used to estimate the growth rate. The orange dashed line shows the fit to the signal. b) Extracted growth rates and the PVM prediction from Eq. (12) as a function of the mode number. All simulation parameters are the same as in Fig. 3 and for ∆w = 12.

Figure 5: Growth rates of KHI modes, normalized to the maximal growth rate predicted by the point-vortex model (PVM), as a function of mode number m (scaled to ∆w), from the UFG regime (a–b) to the BCS regime (c–d), at T = 0 (a, c) and T = 0.3 Tc (b, d). Different colors indicate different values of ∆w = 12, 14, 16. Black lines show the PVM predictions, which are expected to peak at m = ∆w/2. Error bars represent the standard deviation of growth rates extracted from fits over randomly chosen time windows within the instability interval.
